topics.title: The Nile River
topics.short: Egypt was a long, narrow green strip along the Nile, with dry desert on both sides.
topics.trouble: Many children picture Egypt as all sand, or as a jungle. People lived on a thin green ribbon of farmland beside the river, with desert all around it.

topics.title: A River That Flows North
topics.short: The Nile flows from south to north and empties into the Mediterranean Sea through the Delta.
topics.trouble: On a map, north is up, so children often think rivers flow "down" the map to the south. The Nile flows north, up the map.

topics.title: Upper and Lower Egypt
topics.short: Upper Egypt is the south, up the river; Lower Egypt is the north, where the Delta spreads out.
topics.trouble: It seems backward: "Upper" Egypt is at the bottom of the map. The names come from going up the river (south) and down the river (north).

topics.title: The Yearly Flood
topics.short: Every summer the Nile rose over its banks and left rich, dark mud that made the fields fertile.
topics.trouble: Children think the flood was a disaster. Egyptians welcomed it: a good flood meant a good harvest; a low flood meant hunger.

topics.title: Three Seasons
topics.short: The Egyptian year had three seasons: the flood (Akhet), growing (Peret) and harvest (Shemu).
topics.trouble: Children expect four seasons like ours. Egypt's three seasons followed the river, not the weather.

topics.title: Boats on the Nile
topics.short: The Nile was Egypt's road: boats floated north with the current and sailed south with the wind.
topics.trouble: Children think boats needed sails both ways. Going north, the current carried them; going south, the north wind filled the sails.

topics.title: Farming by the River
topics.short: Farmers grew wheat, barley and flax in the black mud and lifted water with a bucket on a pole, the shaduf.
topics.trouble: Children think Egyptians farmed in the sand. Farms were only where the flood reached; the desert stayed dry.

topics.title: What Is a Pharaoh?
topics.short: A pharaoh was the king (or sometimes queen) of all Egypt; the word comes from per-aa, "Great House".
topics.trouble: Children think "Pharaoh" was one person's name. It is a title, like "king", and Egyptians mostly said nesu, "king".

topics.title: Crowns, Crook and Flail
topics.short: The white crown stood for Upper Egypt, the red crown for Lower Egypt, and the double crown for both; kings held a crook and a flail.
topics.trouble: Children mix up the crowns. The tall white crown is Upper Egypt (south); the red crown with a curl is Lower Egypt (north).

topics.title: One Kingdom
topics.short: Around 3000 BC, Upper and Lower Egypt were joined into one kingdom; a carved palette shows King Narmer wearing the white crown of Upper Egypt on one side and the red crown of Lower Egypt on the other.
topics.trouble: Children think Egypt was always one country. It began as smaller lands that were joined together.

topics.title: Hatshepsut, a Woman King
topics.short: Hatshepsut ruled Egypt as king for about fifteen years, built a great temple and sent ships to the land of Punt.
topics.trouble: Children think only men could be pharaoh. A few women ruled, and Hatshepsut is the most famous of them.

topics.title: Ramesses the Great
topics.short: Ramesses II ruled for 66 years, built huge temples like Abu Simbel, and had many children.
topics.trouble: Children think one pharaoh ruled for all of history. There were hundreds of kings over about three thousand years.

topics.title: Tutankhamun, the Boy King
topics.short: Tutankhamun became king at about nine and died young; his small tomb was found nearly untouched in 1922.
topics.trouble: Children think Tutankhamun was the greatest pharaoh. He was a minor king; he is famous because his tomb was found full of treasure.

topics.title: Cleopatra, the Last Pharaoh
topics.short: Cleopatra VII was the last ruler of a Greek family that ruled Egypt; after her, Egypt became part of the Roman Empire.
topics.trouble: Children think Cleopatra lived when the pyramids were built. She lived more than 2,000 years after the Great Pyramid, closer in time to us than to its builders.

topics.title: Why Pyramids?
topics.short: Pyramids were tombs for kings, built to protect the king's body and help him live forever.
topics.trouble: Children think pyramids were palaces or storehouses. They were royal tombs with temples beside them.

topics.title: From Steps to Smooth Sides
topics.short: The first pyramid, King Djoser's, had steps; later kings like Sneferu and Khufu built smooth-sided pyramids.
topics.trouble: Children think every pyramid looks the same. Builders tried steps, a bent angle, and then smooth sides.

topics.title: The Pyramids of Giza and the Sphinx
topics.short: Three great pyramids at Giza belong to Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure; the Great Sphinx guards them.
topics.trouble: Children think the Sphinx is in the desert far from the pyramids. It sits beside Khafre's pyramid at Giza.

topics.title: How They Were Built
topics.short: Teams of skilled Egyptian workers cut stone with copper tools, dragged it on sledges and raised it on ramps; just how the ramps ran is still unknown.
topics.trouble: Many people think slaves built the pyramids, or that the Egyptians had help from someone else. Archaeologists found the workers' town, bakeries and tombs: Egyptians built them.

topics.title: Many Gods
topics.short: The Egyptians believed in many gods, each caring for part of the world: the sun, the river, the sky, the home.
topics.trouble: Children think the gods were only animals. Egyptians pictured many gods as people with animal heads, to show what each god was like.

topics.title: Gods with Animal Heads
topics.short: You can tell gods apart by their heads: Horus the falcon, Anubis the jackal, Thoth the ibis, Bastet the cat, Hathor the cow, Sobek the crocodile.
topics.trouble: Children mix up Anubis (a jackal, like a wild dog) and Bastet (a cat), or Horus (a falcon) and Thoth (an ibis, with a long curved beak).

topics.title: The Story of Osiris and Isis
topics.short: In the old story, Osiris was a good king; his wife Isis brought him back to rule the land of the dead, and their son Horus became king.
topics.trouble: Children think Osiris was the god of evil because he rules the dead. To Egyptians he was a kind king who gave new life.

topics.title: Mummies
topics.short: Egyptians dried and wrapped the bodies of the dead so they would last for the afterlife; this is called mummification.
topics.trouble: Children think mummies are monsters from movies. A mummy is a person whose body was carefully kept, with love, by their family.

topics.title: Tombs and Grave Goods
topics.short: Tombs held food, furniture, games and little helper figures called shabtis for life after death.
topics.trouble: Children think only kings had tombs. Many families had tombs too, from simple graves to painted rooms.

topics.title: The Weighing of the Heart
topics.short: Egyptians believed a dead person's heart was weighed against the feather of Maat, truth, to see if they had lived a good life.
topics.trouble: Children think the heart had to be heavy to pass. A heart as light as the feather, free of wrongdoing, passed.

topics.title: Homes and Families
topics.short: Most families lived in houses of mud brick, with a flat roof for sleeping on hot nights.
topics.trouble: Children think people lived in stone buildings like temples. Stone was for gods and tombs; houses were mud brick.

topics.title: Bread, Beer and Onions
topics.short: Everyday food was bread, thick beer, onions, beans, fish and fruit like dates and figs.
topics.trouble: Children think Egyptians ate like kings every day. Most people ate simple bread and vegetables, and meat on feast days.

topics.title: Clothes, Wigs and Eye Paint
topics.short: People wore light linen clothes; many wore wigs, and men and women lined their eyes with dark paint.
topics.trouble: Children think only women wore eye paint. Men and women both did.

topics.title: Toys and Games
topics.short: Children played with balls, dolls and toy animals, and families played board games such as senet.
topics.trouble: Children think ancient kids had no toys. Archaeologists have found balls, spinning tops and board games.

topics.title: Jobs Along the Nile
topics.short: Most people were farmers; others were bakers, potters, builders, painters, soldiers, priests and scribes.
topics.trouble: Children think everyone in Egypt was a pharaoh or a slave. Most people were farmers and craftspeople.

topics.title: Scribes and School
topics.short: Scribes learned to read and write at school, using reed pens, ink and sheets of papyrus.
topics.trouble: Children think everyone could read. Only a small number of people, mostly scribes, learned to read and write.

topics.title: Signs for Sounds
topics.short: Many hieroglyphs stand for sounds: the owl is m, the water is n, the mouth is r.
topics.trouble: Children think every hieroglyph is a picture of the word. Many signs just stand for sounds, like letters.

topics.title: Signs for Ideas
topics.short: Some signs show what a word means, and some go at the end of a word to give a hint, like walking legs for "go".
topics.trouble: Children try to say every sign. Hint signs at the end of a word are not said out loud.

topics.title: Which Way to Read
topics.short: Hieroglyphs can go left to right, right to left or top to bottom; people and animals face the start of the line.
topics.trouble: Children always start on the left. Look at which way the birds face, and start from that side.

topics.title: Write Your Name
topics.short: You can write your name with sound signs, one sign for each sound.
topics.trouble: Children write one sign for every letter, even silent ones. Write the sounds you hear; Egyptians left out most vowels.

topics.title: Reading a Cartouche
topics.short: A cartouche is an oval loop around a king's or queen's name.
topics.trouble: Children think every word in a loop is a king's name. Cartouches hold only royal names.

topics.title: Egyptian Numbers
topics.short: Egyptians wrote numbers with a stroke for 1, a hobble for 10, a coil of rope for 100 and a lotus for 1,000, repeating signs to add up.
topics.trouble: Children read the signs by place, like our digits. Egyptian numbers just add up: three coils and two hobbles is 320.

topics.title: The Rosetta Stone
topics.short: The Rosetta Stone has the same message in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, which helped people read hieroglyphs again.
topics.trouble: Children think the stone is a dictionary. It is one priestly decree from 196 BC, copied in three scripts.

topics.title: Champollion Cracks the Code
topics.short: In 1822, Jean-François Champollion showed how hieroglyphs work, using names in cartouches and the Coptic language.
topics.trouble: Children think one person read the stone in a day. It took many scholars many years; Thomas Young made early steps, and Champollion cracked it.

topics.title: Finding Tutankhamun's Tomb
topics.short: In 1922, Howard Carter found the steps to Tutankhamun's tomb in the Valley of the Kings, full of treasures.
topics.trouble: Many people believe in a "curse" on the tomb. Most of the people who entered it lived long lives; there was no curse.

topics.title: What Archaeologists Do
topics.short: Archaeologists dig carefully, write down where everything was found, and study it to learn how people lived.
topics.trouble: Children think archaeologists hunt for treasure. They care most about where things were found and what they teach us.
